Members with bareword, text, integer (also negative), byte-string, bool, float and type keys; maps are closed unless a wildcard member allows more. A `null` (or `nil`) key written with `=>` is a required member like any other; `null: T` is the text key `"null"`.

rows.construct: Tag number given as a type `#6.<type>(t)`
rows.notes: Checked as the root rule, a map field, an array element and a choice alternative: the item must be a tag whose number matches `<type>` (`#6.<uint .le 10>(t)`, `#6.<1 / 2>(t)`) and whose content matches `t`. `#6(t)` accepts any tag. A bignum the decoder returns as an integer counts as tag 2 or 3.

`#M` matches the major type, `#M.N` the additional information of the head (the value or length below 24, the width of its argument for 24-27, 31 for an indefinite length; a float written as a double is `#7.27`), `#7.20`-`#7.23` false, true, null and undefined, other `#7.N` a simple value, `#6` any tag, `#6.N` a tag numbered N (the number is the tag number, not additional information), and `#` any item; as the root rule, field, element or choice alternative. Data given as Python values is taken to be written the preferred way.

rows.construct: Root rules that are not maps or arrays
rows.notes: Primitives with controls, choices, literals and tags work as the root type (#94).
Undefined names (with suggestions), duplicate definitions, wrong generic argument counts, unknown controls and misapplied controls are `SchemaError`s with a position (#70).
Integers (number of bytes), byte and text strings (bytes of UTF-8), with a number or a range argument (#67).

Only the bit positions the argument names may be set, for a `uint` and a `bstr` (the first byte is least significant: bit 8 is the lowest bit of the second byte). The argument is a uint, a range, a choice of them, or a rule or `&(...)` that is. Anything else is a schema error; the message names the stray bit.

The pattern is an XSD regular expression, as RFC 8610 says, translated for Python: the whole text must match, `^` and `$` are ordinary characters, `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, `\i`, `\c`, `\p{...}` and `\P{...}` follow XSD, and a class can subtract another (`[a-z-[aeiou]]`). Unicode categories come from the running Python and only common blocks (`\p{IsGreek}`) are known. A pattern XSD does not have (lazy quantifier, `(?:`, back reference) or an unknown category or block is a schema error naming it.
The byte string must hold one CBOR item matching the argument (named types, structures and generic instances, #127); errors inside it are offset-mapped to the outer bytes.

The byte string must hold a CBOR sequence (RFC 8742) whose items, taken as an array, match the argument, which must be an array type: `bstr .cborseq [* uint]` takes any number of uints, including none. A truncated or malformed item is reported with its number and offset. The error is reported at the byte string, as for `.cbor`.

The data must match the target and the argument, for any target: a primitive, a choice, a rule, a tag, a map or an array (`non-empty<M>` is the generic case, #120). `.within` is checked as `.and`, since only values are validated.

The data must match the target and the argument, for any target: a primitive, a choice, a rule, a tag, a map or an array (`non-empty<M>` is the generic case, #120). `.within` is checked as `.and`, since only values are validated.

Numbers (at least the argument); integers and floats.
The data equals the argument, which must be one value: a literal, `true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined` or a rule that is one. Any other argument is a schema error.

Matches the CBOR `undefined` item and nothing else (not `null`); `any` and `#` match it too.
Booleans do not match; `int` is the 64-bit range, bignums are `biguint`/`bignint`.
Tags 2 and 3 (bignums).

`float16`, `float32` and `float64` follow the encoding of data decoded from bytes (`float16` rejects a float written as a double). A float given as a Python value has no encoding and matches a width it can be written in without loss (`1.5` is `float16`, `1.1` is only `float64`). `float` and the choices accept every float width they name; integers never match.
`int / float`.

`tdate` is tag 0 around an RFC 3339 date-time: the calendar must be valid (no 2021-02-29, no month 13), the time `hh:mm:ss` valid, the offset `Z` or `+hh:mm`. Second 60 is accepted only as 23:59:60 UTC at the end of March, June, September or December. `time` is tag 1 around a number.
Tags 4 and 5 holding `[exponent, mantissa]`.
Tag numbers 21, 22, 23 and 55799.

The tag number, the type of the content and what the content means: `encoded-cbor` is one well-formed CBOR item, `uri` an RFC 3986 URI reference, `b64url` base64url text without padding, `b64legacy` base64 text with padding; for both the unused bits of the last character are 0. `regexp` is checked as a Python `re` pattern (with `(?<name>...)` and `\k<name>` accepted), which approximates PCRE and ECMA-262 but does not accept every construct of either.
The tag number and the type of the content (text) are checked. The text is not parsed as a MIME message (RFC 2045): that needs a MIME parser, so tag 36 is shape-only by design.

rows.construct: Integers (major types 0 and 1, up to 64 bits)
rows.notes: Non-shortest encodings are accepted by `loads()` (`1800` is 0); the optional deterministic check is #95.
Text strings must be valid UTF-8.
Duplicate map keys are rejected (#65); non-string keys keep their type (#88).

All three widths decode to a Python float, and `keep_encoding=True` (the validator's decoding) records the width so `float16`, `float32` and `float64` check it. The encoder writes doubles unless `canonical=True` (shortest form that keeps the value); preferred serialization in non-canonical mode is #96.
Tags decode to `(number, value)` tuples, so a two-element tuple is ambiguous with a tag; a dedicated type is planned (#78). Bignums (2, 3) decode to Python ints in values.

Decoded to the same Python values as definite-length items, with chunks joined; the encoder and typed JSON write them back definite-length. A break with nothing to end, a missing break, a chunk of the wrong type, a map that ends after a key, and an indefinite integer or tag are rejected. `#4.31` and `#5.31` (also `#2.31`, `#3.31`) match them when the data is decoded from bytes.

`undefined` decodes to `UNDEFINED` and the other simple values (0-19, 32-255) to `CBORSimple(n)`; they encode back, keep their type as map keys, and appear in typed JSON as `{"$cbor": "undefined"}` and `{"$cbor": "simple", "$value": n}` (untyped: `null` and the number). The two-byte form below 32 and the reserved informations 28-30 are not well-formed.
`loads()` rejects empty, truncated and trailing data; a sequence API is #77.
Shortest integers and floats, map keys sorted by encoded bytes, definite lengths. The optional §4.2.2 reduction of integral floats is not applied.
`typed=True` keeps byte strings, tags and non-string keys so the JSON converts back to the same CBOR; hardening of the annotations is #79.
Not RFC 8610 grammar: the parser accepts it as an extension and every control applies. Deprecated: each use warns and names the standard spelling, and a later release will reject it (#113).
